system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 8 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2176-01-14 02:42:00 to 2176-01-21 09:00:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with a history of psoriatic arthritis, morbid obesity, diabetes, and prior MSSA abscess was admitted for new bilateral leg swelling and exertional shortness of breath. The swelling began two days prior and was associated with a 20-pound weight gain, coinciding with an increase in gabapentin dose six days earlier. Workup revealed no pulmonary embolism, DVT, heart failure, or infection. The rash on his thighs was determined to be benign folliculitis, not vasculitis or cellulitis. Gabapentin was reduced to the prior dose, Lasix was given for fluid management, and compression stockings were started. Symptoms improved during the stay. He was discharged home with medication adjustments and follow-up plans.
problems: Diabetes with neurological manifestations, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Other and unspecified anticonvulsants causing adverse effects in therapeutic use
Adrenal cortical steroids causing adverse effects in therapeutic use

1) Structure: Axial dual-inversion T1-weighted images of the myocardium were
obtained without spectral fat saturation pre-pulses in 5-mm contiguous slices.
2) Function: Breath-hold cine SSFP images were acquired in the left
ventricular 2-chamber, 4-chamber, horizontal long axis, short axis slices (8-
mm slices with 2-mm gaps), sagittal and coronal orientations of the left
ventricular outflow tract, and aortic valve short axis orientations.
3) Flow: Phase-contrast cine images were obtained transverse to the aorta
(axial plane) and main pulmonary artery (oblique plane).


Findings:
Structure and Function
There was normal epicardial fat distribution. The pericardial thickness was
normal. There were no pericardial or pleural effusions. The origins of the
left main and right coronary arteries were identified in their customary
positions.  The indexed diameters of the ascending and descending thoracic
aorta were normal.  The main pulmonary artery diameter index was mildly
dilated.  The left atrial AP dimension was normal.  The left and right atrial
lengths in the 4-chamber view were moderately enlarged.  The coronary sinus
diameter was normal.
The left ventricular end-diastolic dimension index was normal.  The end-
diastolic volume index was normal.  The calculated left ventricular ejection
fraction was normal at 56% with normal regional systolic function.  The
anteroseptal wall was mildly thickened and the inferolateral wall thickness
was normal. The left ventricular mass index was normal.  The right ventricular
end-diastolic volume index was normal.  The calculated right ventricular
ejection fraction was normal at 57%, with normal free wall motion.
The aortic valve appeared to open well but the number of leaflets could not be
determined.

Quantitative Flow
There was no significant intra-cardiac shunt.  Aortic flow demonstrated no
significant aortic regurgitation.  The calculated mitral valve regurgitant
fraction was consistent with no mitral regurgitation.   The resultant
effective forward LVEF was normal at 56%. The right ventricular stroke volume
and pulmonic flow demonstrated no significant pulmonic and no tricuspid
regurgitation.


Non-Cardiac Findings
There was extensive fat deposition, also seen on recent chest CT.

Impression:
1. Normal left ventricular cavity size with normal regional left ventricular
systolic function.  The LVEF was normal at 56%. The effective forward LVEF was
normal at 56%.
2. Normal right ventricular cavity size and systolic function. The RVEF was
normal at 57%.
3. The indexed diameters of the ascending and descending thoracic aorta were
normal. The main pulmonary artery diameter was mildly dilated, though normal
by index.
4. Bi-atrial enlargement.
5. A note is made of extensive abdominal, mediastinal and subcutaneous fat
deposition.

are not visualized.  There is, however, no evidence of deep vein thrombosis.

evidence of deep vein thrombosis in the right lower extremity.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good evening. I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You're here because of chest pain and worsening shortness of breath. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. Since I got out of the hospital last week, my breathing has gotten worse. Even walking to the bathroom makes me winded.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And the chest pain—when does that happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s sharp, right in the middle, especially when I breathe in. It goes away after I rest for about 10 minutes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any fever, cough, or leg swelling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever or cough. But my legs are still swollen, and they hurt. I’ve also lost about 6 pounds since last discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. We’ll check your oxygen levels and run some tests to make sure your heart and lungs are okay. You had a CT scan last time—this time we’ll do an EKG and some blood work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another echo? Last time they said the images weren’t clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll try again. Your body habitus can make it hard to get good images, but we need to check your heart function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs came back. Troponins are negative—no sign of a heart attack. BNP is low, so heart failure is unlikely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your chest X-ray is clear too. No pneumonia or fluid. But your oxygen level drops a bit with activity, so we’ll keep you on 2 liters of oxygen for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s causing the shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not sure yet. It could be related to your obesity—sometimes a large belly can restrict the diaphragm. We’ll get a cardiac MRI to look more closely at your heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We reviewed your echo. The images were still suboptimal, but your ejection fraction looks normal. The right side of the heart appears mildly enlarged.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean I have pulmonary hypertension?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can’t tell for sure because we couldn’t measure the pressure. That’s why we’re scheduling a cardiac MRI—it gives better images and can assess pressures more accurately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my leg swelling—is that still from the gabapentin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’ve reduced your dose back to what you were on before. We’ve also increased your Lasix to 40 mg daily to help with fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your rash on the chest is improving. We’ll switch you from the gel to a cream for easier application.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’ve also had some diarrhea the past two days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started you on Donnatol for that. Given your history of IBD, we want to make sure it’s not a flare. It should help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this point. It’s mild and responding to treatment. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your cardiac MRI is back. Your heart’s pumping function is normal—LVEF is 56%. No signs of blockages or damage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. The MRI shows bi-atrial enlargement and a mildly dilated pulmonary artery, but overall, your heart is functioning well. The issue likely isn’t cardiac.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Then what is it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We consulted Pulmonary. They think your obesity may be causing a restrictive lung problem—your belly might be limiting how much your lungs can expand.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So losing weight could help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. In the meantime, we’re starting you on Advair and albuterol to see if that improves your breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I used the inhaler this morning. I think I can breathe a little easier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s encouraging. We’ll keep you on it and monitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also did a leg ultrasound to check for clots. The main veins look fine—no DVT.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. My legs still hurt though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The pain could be from swelling or your neuropathy. We’ll keep managing the edema and make sure your gabapentin dose is right.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been having more tingling in my feet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s likely your diabetic neuropathy. We’ll keep your blood sugar well-controlled to help with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your stress test came back normal—no signs of ischemia. That’s one more thing we can rule out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So everything’s pointing to my weight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your symptoms—shortness of breath, chest pain with breathing, swelling—fit with a restrictive pattern due to obesity. We’ll set you up with Pulmonary for more testing after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my CPAP? I think I sleep better with BiPAP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You mentioned that, and it makes sense. We’re recommending you follow up with your sleep specialist to switch to home BiPAP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Your breathing has improved, and your legs are less swollen. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What meds will I be on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re lowering your metoprolol and hydrochlorothiazide. Gabapentin is now 300 mg three times a day. You’ll continue Lasix at 40 mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the new inhaler?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—Advair twice a day and albuterol as needed. We’ll send a prescription with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need more tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Pulmonary will do lung function tests to confirm the restriction. And your primary doctor will monitor your heart with follow-up echos.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my diabetes? My sugars have been lower here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good point. You’ve eaten less in the hospital, so your insulin needs were lower. When you go home, you may need to increase your doses. Talk to your endocrinologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s improved. Keep taking Donnatol as needed. If it returns, call your GI doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been worried about the chest pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But all the tests show your heart is healthy. The pain with breathing is likely musculoskeletal or due to restricted movement from obesity.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’ll try to lose weight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That will help a lot. We’ll also refer you to nutrition and weight management.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. Your condition is stable, and we’ve arranged your follow-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: take your inhalers, monitor your breathing, and follow up with Pulmonary and your PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll call if my legs swell or I have chest pain again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. But based on everything, you’re on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with a history of morbid obesity, psoriatic arthritis, obstructive sleep apnea, and type 2 diabetes was admitted for worsening shortness of breath and exertional chest pain following a recent hospitalization for edema. Initial workup ruled out cardiac ischemia, pulmonary embolism, and heart failure. Echocardiogram was suboptimal, but cardiac MRI and stress testing showed normal left and right ventricular function with no evidence of ischemia. Bi-atrial enlargement and mild pulmonary artery dilation were noted, but symptoms were determined to be non-cardiac. Pulmonary consultation suggested a restrictive ventilatory defect due to obesity. The patient's edema improved with furosemide, gabapentin was dose-reduced, and new respiratory symptoms were managed with inhaled bronchodilators. Diarrhea developed during admission and responded to Donnatol. He was discharged home on optimized medical therapy with plans for outpatient pulmonary follow-up and weight management.
